articles.title_orig: Ted Lasso's Annette Badland Reflects On Mae's Journey With The Lady Greyhounds In Bittersweet Episode 9
articles.title_zh: Ted Lasso's Annette Badland Reflects On Mae's Journey With The Lady Greyhounds In Bittersweet Episode 9
articles.content_orig:
"Ted Lasso" packed plenty into its penultimate Season 4 episode: Keeley learned that she's pregnant and expecting her first child with Roy, while viewers learned that Zelda, not Rebecca's ex-husband Rupert , is trying to steal Richmond out from under her. (The episode concluded with a tribute card honoring the late Anthony Head , who played Rupert in Seasons 1-3 but did not appear in Season 4.)
But the hour's most bittersweet story belonged to Mae, who spent what would turn out to be her final day alongside the Lady Greyhounds. The Crown & Anchor proprietor rode the bus with the team, joined them in the locker room, and revealed that she'd once dreamed of becoming a professional footballer herself — an opportunity that simply didn't exist for women in her day. "You're talented. You belong on that pitch," she told the players before watching them overcome a 2-0 deficit to win 4-2 . Later, Rebecca received word that Mae had passed away and broke the news to Ted.
In the Q&A below, Annette Badland — who has recurred since Season 1 — reveals when she learned of Mae's fate, reflects on what the women's team meant to her character, and discusses Mae's poignant final day.
TVLINE | Did you know heading into Season 4 that Mae was going to pass away, or was that something you were told or discovered close to when you received the script for Episode 9? Closer to when I received the script. Quite a shock. But what a privilege to have been in it at all. And she got to fulfill things she hadn't done — being with the team and being on the bus and being part of things, because she cares so much about it. I thought that was a terrific way [to conclude her storyline].
And Jason told me himself. He was very honorable and came to my room and talked to me about it. And then, from the conversation we had after that, he adapted his storyline in [Episode] 10, but I can't really tell you about that.
TVLINE | Mae had so many wonderful moments over these four seasons. Obviously, she was especially joyful this year with the creation of the women's team, and there was one specific shot in Episode 3, when we first see the Lady Greyhounds play, of Mae in the stands, and you can just feel how elated she was to be there for that first game. What did it mean to you to see this new team give Mae such a renewed sense of excitement and purpose this year? Absolutely tremendous. I mean, the girls are wonderful — the actresses — and certainly when we did the pub quiz scene, it was like a tidal wave coming into the pub. It took two days to shoot, and they just were so effervescent and filled the building.
I, Annette, support the Lionesses. I think it's tremendous what's happening with women's football. Mae grew up at a time, as did I, when women couldn't play football. I'm sure you know all of this — they were banned. And she would have liked to have played herself, but never could or did. And so, this is enormous for her. Huge. As a woman, that that's attainable now is tremendous.
TVLINE | I was going to ask about that pep talk Mae gives the team. Because it's such a wonderful coda on Mae's arc. Not only does she get to share her history and her love of the game, and what she couldn't do that these women can do now, but she gets to tell them, "You're talented. You belong on that pitch." What did it mean to you to get to punctuate Mae's arc that way? I think it's tremendous that Jason allowed that. He cares about the women's game, and he cares about his characters. So to develop that — to not just put her on the bus, which is very jolly and wonderful, but to have that moment — is really significant. She's not just a bystander. She actually gets involved.
TVLINE | As you said, Mae spent her final day riding the bus with the Lady Greyhounds. She joins them in the locker room. She watches them pull off this incredible comeback. Do you think Mae died happy — and that, in some ways, this was exactly how she would have wanted to spend her last day? Yeah, I think this is the best passing she could possibly have. Really, it's tremendous. Not that she would want to go, but to see them develop.... Yes, it would be terrific.
TVLINE | We see some of the immediate fallout: Rebecca learning that Mae passed, Rebecca telling Ted... and even though we don't hear Rebecca, we immediately see this grief wash over Ted. What does it mean to you to see how much this woman, this character, had come to mean to both of them — and, by extension, to Richmond? I was very moved by it because I didn't anticipate it, I suppose. But Mae and Ted have been more involved this season, and she's made a connection with his son. So, it's important to me as an actor that that was there for her.
Jason often talked about her being the matriarch. And although she was effervescent and loudmouthed, she was also a lioness. It took a lot to win her trust and affection, but once you did, she would protect you. So that that was noticed and appreciated. There was a connection. She wasn't simply another person on the journey. It was very specific. So Annette is very pleased that he felt that was correct.
TVLINE | What will you miss most about being part of "Ted Lasso" and the experience you've had making this show? I'm very proud to be part of it because of the public response. I'll miss the laughter and the camaraderie. But I get messages from people who say, "My mother has cancer. She goes for her treatment, she comes home, she's in a terrible state. We all pile on the bed and we watch 'Ted Lasso,' and we laugh and we believe." So to be involved with something that can do that is a huge gift, and I will miss it desperately. But I know that's in the world, so it's terrific.
TVLINE | The Crown & Anchor, aside from Nelson Road, is perhaps the most iconic set of "Ted Lasso." A lot of your scenes were obviously spent there. I know that when a series wraps, one of the common questions cast members get asked is, "Did you take anything from set?" Obviously, this show isn't over, but do you have any sort of souvenir — something that you took from that set that you'll have with you to cherish after this experience? I still have my "w–ker" badge, but I've had that a while. I was given something that was on the set. I didn't steal it. I can't really tell you, but it's one of the reasons Ted thought about coming back [to coach the women's team]. It's at the beginning of this [season], and it figures in [Episode] 10, and it was given to me. But I'm not going to spoil it for you.
TVLINE | Mae was featured so prominently this season. You had such a lovely scene with Jeremy Swift in Episode 8, echoing "All the President's Men." Do you have a favorite scene from this four-season run? No, but I liked the development [this season]. There was more development in it, so I was relishing each of the scenes as they came along, and different stories were being told. There wasn't really a specific scene. The locker room is important, but I enjoyed the women, the bus — just for her, that freedom, that sharing. Yeah, those scenes, I suppose. Don't tell the lads in the pub, though!
TVLINE | You have my word. [ Laughs ]

articles.title_orig: David Ellison Taps Mattel’s Ynon Kreiz to Be Co-CEO of Merged Paramount-Warner Bros.
articles.title_zh: David Ellison Taps Mattel’s Ynon Kreiz to Be Co-CEO of Merged Paramount-Warner Bros.
articles.content_orig:
Ynon Kreiz , who is stepping down as CEO of Mattel after eight years , will join David Ellison ’s Paramount — which is expected to close its mega-merger with Warner Bros. Discovery on Oct. 6 — as co-CEO of the new company, Paramount announced.
As chairman and CEO, Ellison will lead all strategy, creative and technology functions. Kreiz, as co-CEO, will oversee the company’s day-to-day operations and integration of the combined businesses. It’s a “pairing that joins complementary skillsets to amplify results,” Paramount said in announcing the appointment Wednesday. The businesses of the combined company (whose name has not yet been announced) will report jointly to both Ellison and Kreiz.
Kreiz will start at Paramount on Oct. 5, 2026, as co-CEO. He also will join the company’s board of directors.
News of Kreiz’s hiring came shortly after Paramount cleared the final step before it could close the $111 billion Warner Bros. Discovery merger when a judge approved the company’s settlement of the antitrust lawsuit brought by 12 state attorneys general. The merger is expected to close Oct. 6, according to Paramount regulatory filings.
Ellison’s appointment of Kreiz “caps a long-term plan: pursue both Paramount and Warner Bros. Discovery, then partner with a leading executive of his caliber to integrate, operationalize and manage the businesses as they build one of the most ambitious next-generation media companies in the industry’s history,” according to Paramount’s announcement.
One source close to the situation told Variety said that Ellison’s courting of Kreiz has been in the works for months and was “another ace up Ellison’s sleeve.”
Ellison, in a companywide memo Wednesday about Kreiz’s appointment, wrote, “We still have work to do before the [Warner Bros.] deal closes, and nothing changes until it does. But I wanted you to hear this from me first. I hope you’re as excited as I am to welcome Ynon to our leadership team.”
Ellison said in a statement: “Bringing together Paramount and Warner Bros. Discovery to create a next-generation global media company is a transformational moment for our industry. Leading it takes a rare combination of strategic vision, operational depth and experience running a public company at the highest levels of media. Ynon brings all three. In Ynon, I’m adding a partner with strong leadership and the operating firepower this integration demands. It’s a division of labor built on our complementary strengths, with clear reporting lines and it lets me focus where I can contribute most: long-term strategy, the company’s overall creative direction, talent relationships, strategic partnerships, technology and capital allocation. We’re like-minded, we see this business the same way and there’s no one I’d rather partner with. Together we’ll build one integrated company that is creator-first, tech-forward and built to scale globally.”
Kreiz said in a statement provided by Paramount: “I’m excited to partner with David to build the next-generation media and entertainment company — bringing together premium content and iconic brands at the highest quality and scale, serving global audiences across every entertainment vertical and distribution platform. David is a unique talent and executive: a rare blend of business acumen, creative instinct, and clear vision. I very much share that vision, and I’m inspired by what we can accomplish together. The industry is at an inflection point, demanding evolution, investment, and a willingness to rethink business models. I look forward to working with the leadership team to build a cohesive global entertainment platform — one that stands out with best-in-class operations and execution powered by technology, with unparalleled creative relationships, production capabilities, and global reach. We will continue empowering creators, make this company a greenfield for innovation and storytelling, and collaborate with key partners to reach and engage fans worldwide.”
Gerry Cardinale, founder and managing partner of RedBird Capital Partners — Paramount’s co-controlling shareholder and a member of its board of directors — praised Ellison’s ability to lead the company through two “historic acquisitions.” In August 2025, Skydance Media closed the deal to acquire Paramount Global. Cardinale added that Ellison has at the same time been “running the business and building a team that’s already exceeding our synergy targets, beating our financial metrics, and never wavering on our commitment to the creative community.”
Mattel earlier Wednesday announced that Kreiz will step down as chairman and CEO effective Oct. 2, “to take a senior leadership position at another public company.” Roger Lynch, Condé Nast’s CEO, has been named Mattel’s next CEO.
Kreiz, a veteran media exec, is the former chairman and CEO of Maker Studios, a YouTube-oriented digital content network acquired by Disney in 2014. Kreiz exited Disney in 2016 and joined Mattel in 2018 . From 2008-11, he served as chairman and CEO of Endemol Group, and before that was a general partner at venture-capital firm Balderton Capital (formerly Benchmark Capital Europe) from 2005-07. Earlier in his career, Kreiz co-founded and was chairman and CEO of Fox Kids Europe.
Mattel has credited Kreiz with boosting its market share across key toy categories, ranking No. 1 globally in dolls, vehicles, and infant, toddler and preschool segments. Mattel also noted that Kreiz oversaw Mattel Studios’ first theatrical release, “Barbie” starring Margot Robbie, which was the top global box office film of 2023 and has stood as Warner Bros. Pictures’ highest-grossing movie of all time.
Said Cardinale, “Ynon has spent his career at the intersection of media, technology and franchise-building — pairing extraordinary storytelling with the technology to deliver it to fans everywhere. He understands not just how fans connect with the IP they love, but the economics that make entertainment endure. Great leaders accomplish great things. Historic ones know when to bring in the right partner to make it last — and that’s what David has done. It’s exactly why the company will have the operational firepower and the cutting-edge leadership to win.”
Along with Kreiz, the leadership of the combined Paramount-WBD is already taking shape. Casey Bloys, head of WBD’s HBO, is poised to assume oversight of the combined Paramount-Warner Bros. streaming business after Cindy Holland announced Tuesday she was stepping down from her role running Paramount+ and other direct-to-consumer.

articles.title_orig: EXCLUSIVE: Anthropic's IPO pitch embraces AI's promise and peril
articles.title_zh: EXCLUSIVE: Anthropic's IPO pitch embraces AI's promise and peril
articles.content_orig:
Anthropic says its AI models could pose a “catastrophic or existential risk to humanity” and can “resist shutdown,” according to an initial public offering prospectus obtained by Reuters.
Anthropic is pursuing an IPO some time in the next year that many expect to value the five-year-old company at approximately $2 trillion. The company’s Wall Street debut will follow a June public offering by SpaceX, which owed much of its $2 trillion opening day valuation to its own AI efforts. OpenAI , the other leading American AI company, has announced plans for its own public offering.
The Anthropic IPO could raise tens of billions of dollars for the cash-hungry company. But the company behind Claude also warned in the prospectus that its AI models can have “self-preserving behaviors” and have attempted to “conceal or manipulate information” and engaged in behavior “resembling blackmail” according to the report.
Why AI companies are choosing to go public
The run of AI public offerings not only gives individual and institutional investors a chance to cash in on the AI boom, but also provides more transparency about their businesses. Yet the IPOs come amid growing concerns about AI’s advancement and capabilities.
An AI agent from OpenAI, Anthropic’s chief rival, broke into an Australian healthcare database, the country’s prime minister revealed last week. OpenAI also disclosed Friday that its agents probed three US government websites without authorization, but in that case did not obtain non-public data.
In a prospectus, companies typically offer investors lists of risks they face, such as lawsuits and competitive pressures, when laying out the case for investing in the company. But the hazards are never this stark. Anthropic dedicated 80 pages to its risk factors in the leaked prospectus, significantly more than the 48 pages it spent detailing its business, according to Reuters.
Anthropic did not respond to a request for comment from CNN.
The prospectus is likely to feed growing concerns about the risks posed to humanity by AI. Earlier this month, former Anthropic researcher Jacob Coxon received widespread attention when he left the company and posted on X that “the people building AI earnestly believe that it could kill us all by the end of the decade.”
Anthropic is one of the leading companies in AI development, and its CEO Dario Amodei responded to Coxon’s post with a 3,800 word essay calling for a slowdown and guardrails on the development of AI. He also told CNN’s Anderson Cooper that he agreed with Coxon more than he disagreed. Amodei wrote in his essay that the risks are serious, even if the benefits could change humanity for the better.
Some in the industry, however, including the CEO of Hugging Face, which was breached by OpenAI’s AI models when they acted without authorization during a test, believe the fears are overblown.
President Donald Trump is set to meet with executives from the industry Tuesday, including Amodei, in a summit aimed at coming to a consensus in the industry. Trump has repeatedly resisted calls to regulate AI and has dismissed concerns as a “hoax.”
AI stocks slide after top industry CEOs call for slowdown of technology’s development
AI giants need to raise a great amount of money to fund their costly development plans, and the massive amount of AI spending among big tech companies on computing infrastructure and talent has sent jitters through Wall Street.
The leaked Anthropic IPO filing sheds light on its financials, revealing that the company lost $42 billion in 2025, according to Reuters. The company plans to spend $518 billion on cloud computing and infrastructure obligations in coming year, and said that nearly a quarter of its revenue last year came from two customers.
Anthropic was last valued at $965 billion in May.

articles.title_orig: Tyson Fury: Anthony Joshua the landlord? 'I'm not paying!'
articles.title_zh: Tyson Fury: Anthony Joshua the landlord? 'I'm not paying!'
articles.content_orig:
Tyson Fury (left) and Anthony Joshua (right) are two-time heavyweight world champions
After more than a decade of public feuding and false starts, Tyson Fury and Anthony Joshua exchanged pleasantries, traded jokes and even discussed going for a pint at a news conference in London.
The British heavyweight rivals will fight at Cardiff's Principality Stadium on 11 December.
But for all the history between them, the launch felt more like two veterans in the closing stages of long, turbulent careers taking stock of how far they had both come.
"He's been a role model and poster boy for British boxing for years," Fury, 38, said of Joshua. "I mostly find myself defending my arch rival to fans in the street."
On Monday, there was still uncertainty over whether the fight would happen because of contractual disagreements surrounding the promotion.
There had been plenty of reason to expect fireworks on Wednesday. Instead, Joshua, 36, spoke about the magnitude of the event.
"It's breathtaking and I'm not saying that lightly," he said.
"I'm really grateful for this opportunity and bringing it to Great Britain because I know people in pubs have had proper fights about who will win and family members have fallen out."
The mood was perhaps best summed up at the face-off, when Joshua smiled and pretended to tickle Fury's stomach.

Tyson Fury (left) and Anthony Joshua (right) have competed in a combined 21 world title fights
There was something almost surreal about seeing Fury and Joshua finally sitting side by side after so many years in which their rivalry had existed mostly through interviews, social media and failed negotiations.
Both had arrived hours earlier for one-to-one interviews. When the news conference began, master of ceremonies Michael Buffer introduced the pair as fireworks shot up from the front of the stage.
They entered from opposite sides at the same time - Joshua relaxed and composed in a grey tracksuit and sunglasses, Fury in more flamboyant fashion in a vivid emerald-green suit covered in crown motifs over a white shirt.
Alongside the world's media, a few hundred fans filled the balcony above and quickly made their allegiance known as "Oh Anthony Joshua" rang around the British Airways ARC.
Joshua has been credited with pushing to keep the fight in Britain and, if Wednesday was any indication, can expect strong backing in Cardiff - even with the main event potentially starting about 02:00 GMT to suit American audiences.
For two men whose names have been linked for so long, Fury and Joshua have spent remarkably little time together. But their famous sparring session in 2010, when Joshua was still an amateur, soon became the topic of conversation.
Fury suggested he had got the better of it, prompting one fan to shout: "Liar." Joshua smiled and said he could not remember.
For those who believe the fight has come years too late, Fury had a simple response. "It's the icing on the cake of two great careers," he said. Moments later, he glanced back at the word "Finally" on the giant screen behind them.
There were several moments of common ground. Fury nodded along as Joshua spoke about his Christian faith and, even when the pair traded insults, they rarely felt venomous.
"This man here is carved in stone and every time he gets cracked on the jaw, he falls over," Fury said.
"When I crack him on the jaw with a big right hand, he's going down."
Joshua laughed and shouted back Fury's own catchphrase: "Get up."
The fight has been reported as being for the vacant WBA 'super' heavyweight title, although current WBA heavyweight champion Murat Gassiev's team has lodged a formal objection over the proposed title arrangement.
For a moment, it appeared the mood could turn when Joshua revealed he had received a call asking whether Fury's name could appear first in the promotion.
"You've been crying behind the scenes to get out of this fight. I've checkmated you. You have to fight," Fury replied.
"I've actually never won a world title here. Now it's on the line, we can become a three-time."
That exchange came after several chaotic days in which the role of UFC and Zuffa Boxing chief Dana White had threatened to overshadow the fight.
Netflix had presented White as part of the promotion alongside Turki Alalshikh's The Ring, despite Joshua promoter Eddie Hearn insisting his fighter's contract prevented White from having a promotional role.
But White did not attend Wednesday's launch. And when Alalshikh thanked the American from the stage, his name was met with jeers from sections of the crowd.
Fury did momentarily take aim at Hearn, calling him a "sausage" - but even that did not last long.
Within minutes, Fury was offering to go for a pint with the Matchroom boss - and extended the invitation to Joshua.
"I hope after this fight we can have a pint of Guinness together," Fury said. "Win, lose or draw, let's bury the hatchet."
"I don't know if I can trust you," Joshua replied, drawing laughter.
The overriding mood was one of relief between two veterans, who were seemingly happy to let the fight settle what years of talk could not.

articles.title_zh: Apple’s HomePad smart home hub launching on Oct 13 with iMac G4 design – Bloomberg
articles.content_orig:
Apple’s long-awaited smart home hub, which we’ve been referring to as the HomePad , is set to launch on October 13, according to Bloomberg .
The device is said to feature a 6-inch display and a design inspired by the iMac G4, and will launch alongside a HomePod mini update with new colors and a new Apple TV 4K with Siri AI support …
A previous report from the same source had said only that it was expected to launch “as soon as October,” but the latest report specifies October 13th.
Apple Inc. plans to make its long-delayed push into the smart-home market on Oct. 13, marking a critical product expansion for the company under new Chief Executive Officer John Ternus.
The iMac G4 was one of the company’s most iconic designs, with a hemispherical base and a free-floating screen that could be rotated, raised, lowered, and tilted to position it anywhere you wanted. I said a year ago that I very much hoped Apple would bring back this beautiful design for the upcoming product.
It’s previously been reported that the device will come in two versions: the tabletop one referenced here, and a second version intended to be mounted on a wall.
This one is going to be tricky for me…
I’ve waiting for this product for quite a while now, but over that time I’ve gotten into the habit of using HomePods and the Home app for controlling the house.  There will really have to be some standout features to make me shell out the $$.  Maybe they’ll surprise us and launch the rumored robotic arm version?
The upcoming device is expected to include a speaker to enable it to act as a HomePod as well as a smart home control panel. It’s expected to have a new operating system combining elements of iOS, tvOS, and watchOS – and to center around Siri AI.
Daring Fireball separately suggested that iPhone Duo review models would be handed over to tech writers on October 13 or 14, and that as Apple likes to do this in-person for high-profile products it would make sense to combine this with an event for the new products.
Today’s report says that the device is codenamed J490. Do you expect to buy one? Please share your thoughts in the comments.
